lesson.title: Phases and conductors: the four-wire measurement

interactive.brief: The one thing you should see is the lead and contact resistance dropping out of the reading when you move the voltage measurement from the meter's own leads to P probes inside the C clamps.
interactive.title: Four wires, three loops
interactive.whatAmILookingAt:
Thirteen screens, with Back and Continue, on phase ID and proving each conductor with a four-wire meter.

Screen 1, Do you still have it? The question: “Three loop readings on one cable: L1 to L2, A = 76.90 mΩ. L2 to L3, B = 80.49 mΩ. L3 to L1, C = 81.16 mΩ. What is L1?” Three choices, in this order: “38.115 mΩ”; “38.785 mΩ”; “38.45 mΩ”. Right, the second: “Still there.” Then the working: “Each loop is two cores in series. L1 = (A + C − B) ÷ 2 = (76.90 + 81.16 − 80.49) ÷ 2 = 77.57 ÷ 2 = 38.785 mΩ.” A last line names the slips: “38.115 mΩ comes from L2's formula, and 38.45 mΩ is half of loop A.” Then two buttons. Refresh the why goes to screen 2, and Skip to the practice goes to screen 8. Wrong, the first: “That comes from L2's formula, (B + A − C) ÷ 2. For L1, add A and C, the two loops that hold L1, then take away B.” Wrong, the third: “That is half of loop A. It is right only if L1 and L2 are equal. Use all three loops.” Then the right working, and on to screen 2.

Screen 2, What it is for. “Phase ID makes sure L1, L2 and L3 are identified, labelled and terminated in the right order. Core resistance proves each conductor end to end, its joints and terminations included. Corrected to 20 °C, each core should be within 2% of its factory value.[^1]” Then phase ID. Assume this order: “Every core starts earthed at both ends, with a technician at each end. Each core is tested in turn to the screen, from both ends.[^2] The far end keeps one core joined to the screen. Under control, it lifts the other two earths. Your end lifts its earths and tests each core to the screen. Only the joined core reads continuity. Then the earths go back on. The two ends then swap jobs and repeat.” The colours: red L1, yellow L2, blue L3. The picture shows three cores side by side. The OSS, your end, is on the left. B01, the far end, is on the right. Each is labelled with its name and colour in words. A screen line runs along each core. At B01, the chosen core is drawn joined to its screen. At the OSS, a continuity tester sits on each core. A control named Far end joins offers L1, L2 and L3. It opens on L1. The joined core reads “continuity” at the OSS, and the other two read “open”. In red, what goes wrong if it is skipped: “Phases terminated in the wrong order can give a short when the cable is energised. A poor joint or termination goes unseen.” The prompt: “Pick which core the far end joins to the screen.” Read: with L1 joined to the screen at B01, only L1 reads continuity at the OSS. So the core marked red at one end is the core marked red at the other. Still: L1 joined, L1 reading continuity, L2 and L3 open.

Screen 3, The why: four wires. “Low resistance usually means under 1 Ω. Down there, the test leads and their contacts can add a big share of what you read. A meter works out resistance as the voltage it sees divided by the current it sends. On two wires, the same leads do both jobs. The current runs through each lead and each contact, and each drops a little voltage. The meter adds those drops to the core's own. Four wires split the jobs. The C leads carry the current, but the meter does not measure across them. The meter measures the voltage on the P leads, but almost no current flows in them. So neither the P leads nor their contacts drop any voltage worth counting.[^3] The reading is whatever carries the current between the two P points.[^4]” The picture shows the DLRO on the left, with four terminals: C1, P1, P2 and C2. Loop A of String B is two cores linked at B01. It is drawn as one long resistor of 339.31 mΩ. Each C lead is drawn with a small resistor of 30 mΩ, and each C clamp's contact with one of 15 mΩ. These are practice values. A stepper named Measure with has three settings: Two wires, P on the C clamps, and P inside the C clamps. The last two use four wires. It opens on Two wires. Current arrows run round the C path. A bracket marked “the meter measures across this” spans everything between the two points where the voltage is taken. The P leads carry no arrow, and a label says “almost no current”. There are two readouts. Meter reads is in mΩ to 2 places. Above the loop is in % to 2 places. On two wires, both leads and both contacts sit inside the bracket. So the meter reads 339.31 + 2 × 30 + 2 × 15 = 429.31 mΩ, 26.52% high. With the P probes clipped on the C clamps, outside their contacts, the leads drop out. The two contacts stay inside. So it reads 339.31 + 2 × 15 = 369.31 mΩ, 8.84% high. With the P probes inside the C clamps, facing each other, only the loop is inside. So it reads 339.31 mΩ, 0.00% above. The words under it: “P on the C clamps still reads 8.84% high. That is far more than the 2% a core is allowed.” The prompt: “Step from two wires to four, then move the P probes inside the C clamps.” Read: two wires read 429.31 mΩ, 26.52% high. Both leads and both contacts carry the current inside the measured stretch. P probes clipped on the C clamps leave the leads out, but the contacts still add 8.84%. P probes inside the C clamps, facing each other, read the loop alone: 339.31 mΩ. Still: P inside the C clamps, reading 339.31 mΩ.

Screen 4, Check. “You measure loop A, 339.31 mΩ, with four wires. Then you swap all four 5 m leads for 30 m ones, so the meter can sit further back. What does the reading do?” Choices: “It rises by the extra lead resistance”; “It stays at 339.31 mΩ”; “It rises by the extra C lead resistance only”. Right, the second: “Almost no current flows in the P leads, so 30 m of P lead drops almost no voltage. The C leads carry the current, but the meter does not measure across them. So the reading holds.” Wrong, the first: “That is a two-wire meter. The P leads carry almost no current, and the meter does not measure across the C leads.” Wrong, the third: “The C leads carry the current, but the meter does not measure across them. So their extra length does not join the reading.”

Screen 5, Three loops, three cores. “Your leads cannot reach both ends of a 2.40 km core. So the far end links two cores, and you read the loop they make. Each loop is two cores in series: A = L1 + L2, B = L2 + L3 and C = L1 + L3. Add A and C, and you have L1 twice, plus L2 and L3 once each. Take B away, and L2 and L3 cancel. So L1 = (A + C − B) ÷ 2. L2 = (B + A − C) ÷ 2 and L3 = (C + B − A) ÷ 2 follow the same way. Add all three loops and every core appears twice. So A + B + C = 2 × (L1 + L2 + L3), a quick check on your sums. The link at B01 and its contacts sit between your P points in every loop. Four wires at the OSS cannot leave them out. So each core you work out carries half the link. Fit it short, firm and clean.” The picture: three cores from the OSS on the left to B01 on the right. A stepper named Loop has three settings. A is L1 to L2, B is L2 to L3, and C is L3 to L1. It opens on A. The two cores of the chosen loop carry current arrows out and back, through a link at B01. Each loop's name gives its worked-example reading: A = 76.90, B = 80.49 and C = 81.16 mΩ. The third core is drawn earthed at both ends. Under the picture sit the three formulas. The chosen loop's letter is lit in each. The prompt: “Step through the three loops.” Read: loop A links L1 and L2 at B01, so it reads L1 + L2. Loop B reads L2 + L3, and loop C reads L1 + L3. So L1 = (A + C − B) ÷ 2, L2 = (B + A − C) ÷ 2 and L3 = (C + B − A) ÷ 2. With the worked example's readings, A + B + C = 238.55 mΩ, twice the three cores together. Still: all three loops drawn at once, each labelled with its pair of cores.

Screen 6, Worked example, a line at each press. The loops: A = 76.90, B = 80.49 and C = 81.16 mΩ. The prompt: “Work each line yourself first, then press Show.” Line 1: “L1 = (76.90 + 81.16 − 80.49) ÷ 2 = 77.57 ÷ 2 = 38.785 mΩ.” Line 2: “L2 = (80.49 + 76.90 − 81.16) ÷ 2 = 76.23 ÷ 2 = 38.115 mΩ.” Line 3: “L3 = (81.16 + 80.49 − 76.90) ÷ 2 = 84.75 ÷ 2 = 42.375 mΩ.” Line 4: “Check: (76.90 + 80.49 + 81.16) ÷ 2 = 238.55 ÷ 2 = 119.275 mΩ. And 38.785 + 38.115 + 42.375 = 119.275 mΩ.” A note under the lines: “Name each result by its core, never by a loop letter.” Then: “L3 reads 9.26% above L1 and 11.18% above L2. Three cores of one cable have the same size and length, so they should read close together. Find out why before you submit a gap like this.” Read: L1 = 38.785 mΩ, L2 = 38.115 mΩ and L3 = 42.375 mΩ. They add to 119.275 mΩ, half of A + B + C. L3 sits 9.26% above L1 and 11.18% above L2. Explain a gap like that before you submit. Still: all four lines shown, with the note.

Screen 7, A cold cable reads low. “Copper's resistance rises as it warms, by 0.00393 of its 20 °C value for each degree.[^5] That is about 0.4% per °C. Factory values are given at 20 °C. So a cable on the seabed at 12 °C reads low, even when it is sound. Correct the reading to 20 °C before you compare it: R20 = R_t ÷ (1 + 0.00393 × (t − 20)).” The picture: a thermometer and two bars. The first bar is L1's factory value, 174.70 mΩ at 20 °C, a practice value. The second bar is what the DLRO reads on that same sound core at the slider's temperature. A band round the first bar marks 2% either side. A Cable temperature slider runs from 4 to 30 °C in steps of 1 °C. It opens at 20 °C. There are two readouts. DLRO reads = 174.70 × (1 + 0.00393 × (t − 20)), in mΩ to 2 places. Against the certificate = 0.393 × (t − 20), in % to 2 places. At 20 °C it reads 174.70 mΩ, 0.00%. At 12 °C it reads 169.21 mΩ, −3.14%, outside the band. A red line says “A sound core that looks like a fail.” At 4 °C it reads 163.71 mΩ, −6.29%. At 30 °C it reads 181.57 mΩ, +3.93%. The reading leaves the band near 15 °C and near 25 °C. A line under it at 12 °C: “Corrected: 169.21 ÷ 0.96856 = 174.70 mΩ, right on its certificate.” The prompt: “Drag the temperature down to 12 °C.” Read: L1's factory value is 174.70 mΩ at 20 °C. At 12 °C the same sound core reads 169.21 mΩ, 3.14% low and outside 2%. Divide by 1 + 0.00393 × (12 − 20) = 0.96856 and it is back to 174.70 mΩ. About 5 °C either side of 20 °C uses up the whole 2%. Still: 12 °C, reading 169.21 mΩ, −3.14%, with the corrected line shown.

Screen 8, Section A, question 2 (a). The scenario panel. Then the test, said once: “String B is at 12 °C. Your end is the OSS. Each pair is linked at B01 in turn, and the DLRO reads: L1 to L2, A = 339.31 mΩ. L2 to L3, B = 339.21 mΩ. L1 to L3, C = 338.32 mΩ. These are practice values, kept to 0.01 mΩ for the working.” The question: “(a) Determine the resistance of core L2 at 12 °C.” A typed answer, part 2a: (339.21 + 339.31 − 338.32) ÷ 2 = 340.20 ÷ 2 = 170.10 mΩ, to 2 places. Slips: 340.20 mΩ, “That is two cores' worth. Halve it.” 169.21 mΩ, “That comes from L1's formula. For L2, add A and B, the two loops that hold L2, then take away C.” 169.66 mΩ, “That is half of loop A. It assumes L1 and L2 are equal.” After two misses, the working. Then one line: “L1 and L3 work out the same way, at 169.21 and 169.11 mΩ.”

Screen 9, Section A, question 2 (b). Part (a) carried forward: 170.10 mΩ. “The factory certificate gives each core at 20 °C: L1 174.70, L2 174.90 and L3 174.60 mΩ. These are practice values. Take copper's coefficient as 0.00393 per °C. (b) Determine L2's resistance corrected to 20 °C.” A typed answer, part 2b: 1 + 0.00393 × (12 − 20) = 0.96856, then 170.10 ÷ 0.96856 = 175.62 mΩ. 175.72 mΩ is accepted too. It comes from about 0.4% per °C: 170.10 ÷ 0.968. Slips: 164.75 mΩ, “You multiplied by 0.96856. A cold core reads low, so its 20 °C value is higher. Divide.” 170.10 mΩ, “That is the reading at 12 °C. Correct it to 20 °C first.” After two misses, the working.

Screen 10, Section A, question 2 (c). Parts (a) and (b) carried forward. “(c) Determine L2's deviation from its factory value of 174.90 mΩ, as a percentage.” A typed answer, part 2c: (175.62 − 174.90) ÷ 174.90 × 100 = +0.41%. That is inside 2%, so it is acceptable. 0.47% is accepted too, from 175.72 mΩ. Slips: −2.74%, “That sets the 12 °C reading against a 20 °C value. Use the corrected 175.62 mΩ.” −0.41%, “That is the factory value minus the reading. Take the reading minus the factory value.” After two misses, the working. Then: “Uncorrected, L2 looks 2.74% low, a false fail. Corrected, it is 0.41% high and passes. L1 and L3 match their certificates exactly. So L2's conductor passes, joints and all. This test does not look at its insulation.”

Screen 11, Section B: “Explain why the P probes must sit inside the C clamps, facing each other.” A written answer, marked against five points. Any three make a full answer. One more go, then the model answer.

Screen 12, Section A, changed numbers. “Another three-core cable is read at 20 °C, so no correction is needed. Its loops: L1 to L2, A = 120.40 mΩ. L2 to L3, B = 121.10 mΩ. L1 to L3, C = 120.90 mΩ. Determine the resistance of core L3.” A typed answer: (120.90 + 121.10 − 120.40) ÷ 2 = 121.60 ÷ 2 = 60.80 mΩ. Slips: 121.60 mΩ, “Halve it. Each loop holds two cores.” 60.10 mΩ, “That comes from L1's formula. For L3, add B and C, then take away A.” Then: “Check: (120.40 + 121.10 + 120.90) ÷ 2 = 181.20 mΩ. The three cores, 60.10, 60.30 and 60.80 mΩ, add to the same.”

Screen 13, Keep this: the summary card, then Finish the lesson.

On the screens with working, a caption says each line is worked from the rounded figures shown before it. Each screen that uses a practice value says so.
interactive.ignores: The leads and contacts are drawn as fixed resistors, with practice values. Real contact resistance changes each time a clamp goes on. The P leads are drawn with no current. In fact a tiny current flows, far too small to move the reading. Each core is drawn as a plain resistor. The meter also reverses its current and averages the two readings, which cancels small thermal voltages. That is not shown. The temperature rule is a straight line from 20 °C. That suits the few degrees either side that a cable sees on a job. Phase ID is drawn with perfect continuity and perfect opens. A real reading has some resistance either way.

explain.text:
Below 1 Ω, the test leads and their contacts can add a big share of what you read. So a DLRO uses four wires. Two C leads carry the test current through the core. Two P leads measure the voltage across it, from inside the C clamps. Three loop readings then give you the three cores. Correct each one to 20 °C, then set it against its factory value.

A meter works out resistance as the voltage it sees divided by the current it sends. On two wires, the same leads do both jobs. The current runs through each lead and each contact, and each drops a little voltage. The meter adds those drops to the core's own. Four wires split the jobs. The C leads still carry the current, but the meter does not measure across them. The meter measures the voltage on the P leads, but almost no current flows in them. So neither the P leads nor their contacts drop any voltage worth counting.[^3] The reading is whatever carries the current between the two P points. That is why the P probes sit inside the C clamps, facing each other. Only the core lies between them.

Your leads cannot reach both ends of a core kilometres long. So the far end links two cores, and you read the loop they make. Each loop is two cores in series: A = L1 + L2, B = L2 + L3 and C = L1 + L3. Add A and C and you have L1 twice, plus L2 and L3 once each. Take away B and those two cancel. So L1 = (A + C − B) ÷ 2, and L2 and L3 follow the same way.

Copper's resistance rises by 0.00393 of its 20 °C value for each degree warmer.[^5] Factory values are given at 20 °C. At 12 °C, a core right on its certificate reads 3.14% low. That looks like a fail. So correct each reading first: R20 = R_t ÷ (1 + 0.00393 × (t − 20)). The pictures are simplified. Real contacts change each time a clamp goes on. The lead and contact values are practice ones.

**Four wires keep the leads out. Three loops give three cores. Corrected to 20 °C, each core should be within 2% of its factory value.[^1]**

analogy.text: You null your low-resistance ohmmeter's leads before an R1+R2 test. That takes the leads' own resistance off every reading. Four wires do the same job without nulling, and they leave out the contacts as well.
analogy.breaks: Nulling removes the leads as they were at the moment you nulled them. The contacts change each time you clip on. A two-wire meter still counts them. Four wires leave out the leads and the contacts on every reading. That is because the P leads carry almost no current.

practice.text:
- Start with every core earthed at both ends, and a technician at each end. Talk to the far end before every change.
- Phase ID: test each core in turn to the screen, from both ends.[^2] With one core joined to the screen at the far end, only that core should read continuity. Check its colour: red L1, yellow L2, blue L3.
- Core resistance, one loop at a time. At the far end, lift the earths on the loop's two cores and link them. Keep the third core earthed. At your end, connect the leads first. Then lift the same two earths, read the loop and earth them again.
- Put the C clamps on the outside and the P probes inside them, facing each other.
- Read loop A, L1 to L2. Then read B, L2 to L3, and C, L3 to L1. After the last loop, remove the link and put every earth back on.
- Work out each core. Check that A + B + C = 2 × (L1 + L2 + L3).
- Note the cable's temperature. Correct each core to 20 °C, then compare it with its factory value.
- If a core is out, find out why before you submit it. Rule out temperature and your connections first.

**Rule of thumb:** copper changes about 0.4% per °C. So about 5 °C away from 20 °C uses up the whole 2%.

**Rule of thumb:** on a DLRO10HD the 10 A range stops at 250 mΩ.[^8] A loop of about 340 mΩ goes on the 1 A range, which reads to 0.1 mΩ. The practice readings keep 0.01 mΩ for the working.

**The range switch:** yellow marks the test current. Green ranges limit the output to 0.25 W. Red ranges can put up to 25 W into what you are testing.

**Worked example:** take String B at 12 °C. Its practice readings are A = 339.31, B = 339.21 and C = 338.32 mΩ. L1 = (339.31 + 338.32 − 339.21) ÷ 2 = 169.21 mΩ. The factor is 1 + 0.00393 × (12 − 20) = 0.96856. So L1 at 20 °C is 169.21 ÷ 0.96856 = 174.70 mΩ. Its certificate says 174.70 mΩ, a deviation of 0.00%.

**Common mistakes**
- P probes clipped onto the C clamps instead of the core inside them. The clamps' contact resistance then joins the reading.
- The wrong loop formula, or half a loop taken as one core.
- A cold reading set against a 20 °C certificate.
- Submitting a core that is out before finding why.
- Lifting an earth without telling the far end.

b1.model: Below 1 Ω, the leads and their contacts can add as much resistance as the core itself. So a two-wire reading can be well out. A four-wire meter splits the jobs. The test current flows through the C leads, and the voltage is measured on the separate P leads. Almost no current flows in the P leads. So their resistance and their contacts' resistance drop almost no voltage. They do not affect the reading. The meter reads the resistance between the two P points. So the P probes go inside the C clamps, facing each other. Then only the core lies between them, and the C clamps' contact resistance is left outside.

interactive.title: Four wires, three loops
interactive.brief: The one thing you should see is the lead and contact resistance dropping out of the reading when you move the voltage measurement from the meter's own leads to P probes inside the C clamps.

checks.label: Two wires read 429.31 mΩ (26.52% high), P on the C clamps 369.31 mΩ (8.84%), P inside the C clamps 339.31 mΩ (0.00%)
Each move of the voltage points inward lowers the reading, and it never reads below the loop
Each conductor is tested in turn using the screen as the return: only the core joined at the far end reads continuity
Worked example: L1 38.785, L2 38.115, L3 42.375 mΩ; they add to 119.275 mΩ, half of A + B + C; L3 is 9.26% and 11.18% above; half of A is 38.45 mΩ
String B at 12 °C: L1 169.21, L2 170.10, L3 169.11 mΩ; A + B + C is twice their sum; slips 340.20 and 169.66 mΩ
The reading leaves the 2% band between 14 and 15 °C and between 25 and 26 °C; about 5 °C either side uses it up
Corrected at 12 °C: 169.21 ÷ 0.96856 = 174.70 mΩ, and the reading rises with every degree
Changed numbers: L3 = 60.80 mΩ, slips 121.60 and 60.10 mΩ; the three cores, 60.10 + 60.30 + 60.80, make 181.20 mΩ
Every slip lies outside its answer's accepted figures
The measured value is between the potential connections: with the P probes inside the C clamps it is the loop alone
Since no current flows in the P leads, the P contacts produce no voltage: the reading holds whatever the P leads are
The temperature coefficient of standard copper is 0.00393 at 20 °C
Low resistance is generally considered under 1 Ω
Measured resistance should be within 2% of factory values

applied.problem: Three absolutes: the notes say low resistance is 'generally' under 1 Ω; crossed phases give a short only where the cable closes onto another supply (otherwise reversed rotation); and 'whatever is wrong with L2' presumes a fault the passing test has not shown.

'A sound core at 12 °C reads 3.14% low' holds only for a core exactly on its certificate (a sound core can sit anywhere within 2%); and the 2.40 km is the practice case's length, unlabelled in a sentence read alone.

Safety order: the notes clamp on before removing the earths, so an unearthed core with induced voltage is never handled; and P probes on the core beyond the C clamps see no current there, so it is P on the clamps, not 'outside', that adds contact resistance.

With the P probes on the core outside the C clamps no current flows between P and C, so the clamps' contact resistance does not join; it joins when the P probes are clipped on the C clamps, as the lesson's own picture shows.
Only a core exactly on its 20 °C certificate reads 3.14% low at 12 °C; a sound core can sit anywhere within 2% of it.

notes.problem: String B's loops (339.31 mΩ etc.) are given to 0.01 mΩ, but the DLRO10HD's 2.5 Ω ranges resolve 0.1 mΩ at ±0.2% ±200 µΩ (about ±0.9 mΩ here), so L2's 0.72 mΩ gap and 'L1 and L3 match exactly' sit inside the meter's accuracy; a 10 mA 2.5 Ω green range also exists.
